agent_notes: The Hebrew verse 1 carries the superscription (KJV 73:0) together with the opening line, so the commentary covers both. 'לברי לבב' is glossed 'to the pure of heart'; the KJV 'even to such as are of a clean heart' adds 'even', which the Hebrew does not have.

אַךְ is a famous crux: 'surely/truly' (affirmation, Meiri, Radak, Metzudat David) or 'only/yet' (restrictive, YLT). I render it 'Surely' in the dramatic layer and keep 'Only' visible in the literal layer, because the psalm's whole turn is that the speaker doubted what he asserts.

The most difficult verse of the window. The Qere ישוב ('returns') and the Ketiv ישיב ('he brings back/turns') differ (Radak, Meiri). Both 'his people' (עמו) and 'hither' (הלם) have been read in many ways, and 'waters of a full [cup]' is elliptical. I translate the Qere literally and say the verse is disputed rather than choosing between Rashi (the people turn to the wicked's way), Radak/Meiri (the people are bewildered, drinking a cup of bitterness) and others. The five English versions split completely here (BBE departs entirely from the others).

agent_notes: Ibn Ezra attributes the saying to God's own people (not the wicked); Rashi, Radak and Meiri take it as the wicked's taunt or the bewildered's doubt. The Hebrew has only 'and they said', with no named subject, and I keep that.

שלוי עולם: 'at ease for ever / of the age'. KJV 'who prosper in the world' interprets עולם as 'the world'; the Hebrew could mean 'always' (ASV, BBE) or 'the world'. I keep 'always at ease' in the literal layer and mention both.
רִיק is an adverbial accusative, 'emptily, for nothing'; I kept 'for nothing' in both layers. KJV 'in vain' is fine, but YLT's 'a vain thing' reads it as a noun.

agent_notes: Hard verse; the medieval commentators (Radak, Meiri) already move הִנֵּה, and the sense is uncertain. I read 'if I had said, I will tell it like them' with 'like them' (כְמוֹ) as the speech of the wicked, and I kept בָגָדְתִּי as 'I would have betrayed' (perfect of certainty in a conditional). KJV 'offend against' softens בָּגַד, which is 'act treacherously'. BBE reads it as an accusation against God, which the Hebrew does not support.

agent_notes: Written הִיא (Ketiv), read הוּא (Qere), as Radak and Meiri note; the packet glosses the reading. I did not take Rashi's reading that עָמָל means 'injustice'; I kept 'toil, trouble' and mention Rashi in the notes as his own gloss.

מִקְדְּשֵׁי is a plural of intensity or 'sanctuaries' (the whole sacred precinct); I kept the plural in the literal layer. Rashi (Sennacherib), Radak and Malbim (afterlife) and Metzudat David (priests who teach there) all read the 'entering' differently. I left the text open: the dramatic layer says only that the speaker entered and understood their end.

agent_notes: Both verbs are Ketiv/Qere pairs: Ketiv נטוי and שפכה (singular, per Radak and Meiri each foot is 'bent', each 'step' poured) against Qere נטיו and שפכו. The glosses follow the Qere (the printed reading); the Ketiv is mentioned in the commentary.

Addressed the request: the two halves are framed by two different verbs of waking, קיץ (hāqîṣ) and עור (ʿûr), not one root. בעיר is ambiguous: 'in the city' (noun עיר, Rashi, Meiri's first reading) or 'in rousing' (infinitive of עור, Radak, Targum, Meiri's second reading). The word table parses it as the verb, and I follow that in both English layers, keeping the city reading in the commentary. Rashi's Sennacherib application (Isa 37:36) is his, not the verse's.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses כִּי as 'if'; I read it as 'when, for' (causal-temporal), with the following imperfects as past habitual, as in KJV 'Thus'. KJV 'reins' for כְּלָיוֹת is archaic English for kidneys, I kept 'kidneys' in the literal layer.

Addressed the request: the accent after אחר supports the KJV's 'afterward … to glory' (Rashi supplies the ל, Radak says אחר stands by itself). The KJV's only addition is the preposition 'to', which Rashi also supplies. Ibn Ezra's 'after this honor, take me' and Radak's 'take my honor = the soul' are given as alternatives. The literal layer keeps the bare 'honor' with a bracketed 'to'. תקחני is not glossed 'to heaven': the text does not say where.

agent_notes: Glossed kalah as 'has come to an end' (finished, spent) with the sense of failing; Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as 'longing' (cf. Ps 119:81, which Rashi cites), the other classical readers as 'failing'. Both are lexically possible; I followed 'fail' in the translations and recorded the other reading in a note. Verse 25 is also the pivot between the speaker's longing and his collapse, so the ambiguity is probably deliberate.

STEPBible parses hitzmatah as 2ms perfect 'you destroy'. The verbal root is tsamat (H6789), 'to silence, cut off'. I rendered it 'you have cut off' in the literal layer, a perfect that the dramatic layer keeps as settled fact. (The verb is hiphil of tsamat; the form's morphology, not the gloss, is what I follow.) The versions split between future ('shall perish') for yoveidu and past for hitzmatah (KJV, ASV); the Hebrew imperfect plus perfect is a general truth, as Ibn Ezra's comparison with Ps 49:11 ('together the fool and the brutish perish') suggests.

agent_notes: Four points: (1) STEPBible glosses qirvat as 'approach of'; I kept 'nearness'. (2) 'Lord YHWH' (adonai YHWH) is glossed as two words as written; the pointing of YHWH here is that of Elohim, to avoid saying 'Adonai Adonai' (a standard masoretic convention, my own statement, not from the packet). The literal layer keeps YHWH; the dramatic layer says 'the Lord GOD' as in KJV for convention. (3) The Targum in the packet reads 'to draw near to the LORD' and 'to tell the righteous all the commands of your mission', a different reading of the end; I did not follow it. (4) The last word malakhotekha is from mela'khah ('work, errand'); Rashi takes it as 'your missions' (what the holy spirit sends him to say), while Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra, like all five versions, take 'works'. I follow 'works'.

חרצבות and אולם are both contested. Rashi, Radak and Meiri take חרצבות as 'bonds, pangs' (compare Isa 58:6); Rashi also records a rabbinic notarikon. For אולם I follow the reading 'body' (so STEPBible), which several commentators support in the form 'strong/sound their body or strength'; others read 'hall/porch' (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion) or 'as a hall'. The literal layer carries 'body' with a bracket for the alternative.
שית is difficult. STEPBible and KJV read 'garment' (the sense is a wrap or attire of violence); Meiri reads 'foundation' and Ibn Ezra 'way' or 'side'. I keep 'garment of' and say so in a note.

agent_notes: Per the reviewer request, 'eyes' is plural in the gloss (pos 3) and the literal layer; the singular verb 'it goes out' agrees with the plural noun as a collective, and the suffix -מוֹ is the archaic poetic 3mp. The verb יצא is read as 'goes out / bulges' (Rashi, Radak), against Meiri, who takes it as 'their colour goes out / shines' and denies that fat makes eyes bulge. I kept the bulging reading, which is the majority one and the one the KJV, ASV and BBE share, and gave Meiri's in the commentary.

משכיות is glossed 'imaginings'. The commentaries split between 'thoughts' (Ibn Ezra citing R. Moshe, Radak, Meiri, from שכוי 'heart/mind', Job 38:36) and 'carved figures' (Ibn Ezra's second suggestion, from מַשְׂכִּית). YLT's 'The imaginations of the heart transgressed' keeps the literal syntax; the KJV 'more than heart could wish' follows Rashi and Malbim.

agent_notes: Per the reviewer request: the Lev 26:39 comparison (ימקו בעוניהם) is Meiri's, who stresses that it is a different root (מקק, geminate) from ימיקו (מוק, hollow verb). Ibn Ezra compares 'המק בשרו' (Zech 14:12), from the geminate root. The verb מוק occurs only here in the Bible, so 'mock' is a context-driven guess; the versions give 'corrupt' (KJV), 'scoff' (ASV), and BBE ignores the verb. I chose 'they mock' from the Rashi/Radak/Meiri sense of dissolving others with words, and gave 'jeer' in the dramatic layer.
